questions.stem: The power to pardon, commute, or remit sentences for offenses against STATE laws is vested in the Governor under which Article of the Constitution?

options.option_text: Article 161
Article 72
Article 153
Article 213

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 161 grants the Governor of a state the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment for offenses against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
DECOY BUSTING: Article 72 gives the pardoning power to the President. Article 153 states that there shall be a Governor for each state. Article 213 gives the Governor the power to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of the legislature.
EXAM INSIGHT: While the Governor has broad pardoning powers, he CANNOT pardon a death sentence (only the President can do that under Art 72), nor can he pardon sentences from a Court-Martial.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who administers the oath of office to the Governor of a State?

options.option_text: The Chief Justice of the concerned State High Court
The President of India
The Chief Minister of the State
The Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Under Article 159, the oath of office to the Governor is administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned State High Court. In his absence, the senior-most judge of that High Court available administers the oath.
DECOY BUSTING: The President APPOINTS the Governor (Article 155), but does NOT administer the oath (unless it's the President's own oath, administered by the CJI). The Chief Minister has no role in appointing or swearing in the Governor.
EXAM INSIGHT: This is a classic trap. Appointment = President. Oath = Chief Justice of the High Court. Similarly, for the President: Appointment = Election. Oath = Chief Justice of India.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: What is the minimum age prescribed by the Constitution for a person to be appointed as the Governor of a State?

options.option_text: 35 years
30 years
25 years
40 years

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 157 states only two primary qualifications for the appointment of a Governor: 1) He should be a citizen of India, and 2) He must have completed the age of 35 years.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- 25 years is the minimum age for a Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA) or Member of Parliament (Lok Sabha).
- 30 years is the minimum age for a Member of Legislative Council (MLC) or Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha).
EXAM INSIGHT: The age requirement (35 years) is exactly the same for the President, Vice-President, and the Governor.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor of an Indian State holds office for what tenure, and whose pleasure determines continuance in that office?

options.option_text: Five years, or at the pleasure of the Prime Minister of India
Five years, but holdable at the pleasure of the President of India
Six years, subject to the pleasure of the Parliament of India
Four years, subject to the pleasure of the Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation: Article 156(1) states the Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President; Article 156(3) fixes the nominal term at five years. The pleasure clause means the President can remove the Governor before the term ends. The Prime Minister (A) is not constitutionally vested with this power directly, though the President conventionally acts on PM's advice.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution specifically empowers the Governor to promulgate Ordinances when the State Legislature is not in session?

options.option_text: Article 123, which grants similar ordinance powers to the President
Article 200, which deals with the Governor giving assent to Bills
Article 213, which covers the Governor's ordinance-promulgation power
Article 356, which provides for imposition of President's Rule in States

questions.explanation: Article 213 is the State-level counterpart of Article 123 (which grants ordinance power to the President, not the Governor). When the State Legislature (or both Houses in a bicameral State) is not in session, the Governor may promulgate an Ordinance with the same force as a State Act. Article 200 (B) deals only with assent to Bills, not Ordinances.

questions.stem: In which of the following situations does the Governor exercise constitutional discretion genuinely independent of the Council of Ministers' advice?

options.option_text: Summoning a session of the State Legislature under Article 174
Appointing the Advocate General of the State after the CoM recommends
Reserving a Bill passed by the State Legislature for the President's consideration
Promulgating an Ordinance under Article 213 based on Cabinet's recommendation

questions.explanation: Under Article 200, the Governor 'may in his discretion' reserve a Bill for the President's consideration — a genuine discretionary act not requiring ministerial advice. In contrast, summoning the Legislature (A), appointing the Advocate General (B), and promulgating Ordinances (D) are all exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 163(1).

questions.stem: Article 167 of the Constitution imposes a constitutional duty on the Chief Minister towards the Governor. Which of the following most accurately describes its full scope?

options.option_text: Communicate only Cabinet decisions involving financial commitments above a prescribed limit
Furnish all Cabinet decisions and any information the Governor calls for on State affairs
Submit monthly written reports on the State's legislative agenda to the Governor
Communicate Cabinet decisions only after implementation to avoid executive interference

questions.explanation: Article 167 requires the CM to (a) communicate all Council of Ministers' decisions to the Governor, (b) furnish any information relating to State administration and proposed legislation the Governor calls for, and (c) if the Governor requires, submit for CoM consideration any matter on which a Minister has decided individually. Option A invents a financial threshold; Option C adds a 'monthly report' obligation that does not exist in the Constitution.

questions.stem: The proviso to Article 200 mandates that the Governor SHALL (not merely may) reserve a Bill passed by the State Legislature for the President's consideration in which specific situation?

options.option_text: When the Bill places restrictions on inter-State freedom of trade or commerce
When in the Governor's opinion the Bill would derogate from the High Court's position
When the Bill proposes amendment of State List subjects that touch the Union List
When the Bill involves expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the State

questions.explanation: The proviso to Article 200 states: '…the Governor shall reserve for the consideration of the President any Bill which in the opinion of the Governor would, if it became law, so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by this Constitution designed to fill.' This is a mandatory reservation unlike the general discretion. Options A, C, and D are common distractors but carry no mandatory-reservation trigger in Article 200.

questions.stem: Under Article 213(2), an Ordinance promulgated by the Governor must be laid before the State Legislature. What is the precise legal consequence if the Legislative Assembly passes a resolution disapproving it before the six-week period expires?

options.option_text: The Ordinance automatically lapses only after the full six-week window expires
The Ordinance ceases to operate from the date the disapproving resolution is passed
The President must counter-sign the resolution for it to nullify the Ordinance
The Governor may re-promulgate the same Ordinance within 30 days of the resolution

questions.explanation: Article 213(2) states an Ordinance ceases to operate either (i) at the expiration of six weeks from reassembly of the Legislature, OR (ii) if before that period a resolution disapproving it is passed — whichever is earlier. The Ordinance ceases immediately upon the resolution, not after waiting out six weeks (A). No Presidential counter-signature is required (C). In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court held that re-promulgating an Ordinance to bypass legislative scrutiny is a constitutional fraud, making option D legally impermissible.

questions.stem: The nine-judge constitutional bench in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) is landmark on Article 356. Which of the following most accurately reflects its core holding regarding the Governor's role?

options.option_text: The Governor's Article 356 report is a political act immune from judicial scrutiny
Governor's Art. 356 satisfaction is reviewable if material lacks rational nexus to breakdown
Once Article 356 is proclaimed, the State Legislature is permanently dissolved by law
The Governor can recommend President's Rule only after consulting the Election Commission

questions.explanation: In S.R. Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court overruled the pre-existing view that Article 356 proclamations are non-justiciable. It held the Governor's report and Presidential satisfaction are subject to judicial review; if the material placed before the President had no rational nexus with the breakdown of constitutional machinery, the proclamation can be struck down. Option A is the pre-Bommai position the court rejected. Option C is wrong — the Legislature is only suspended (not dissolved) upon proclamation; dissolution requires a subsequent order. Option D is not a constitutional requirement.
